title: VertexWave x Redwood — Tiered batching + cost-efficient tier technical deep dive
topics: Cost-efficient tier: what changes vs standard/fast
Latency SLO definitions (p95/p99) and measurement windows
Benchmark methodology and workload corpus representativeness
Rollout controls, opt-in/opt-out, and verifying effective config
questions: Can we set different batching tiers per route (chat streaming vs non-streaming jobs)?
What is the max queue delay in cost-efficient tier, and does it ever violate p95?
How do we validate token cadence doesn’t regress for streaming?
Do tier defaults change per model family or GPU SKU?
What rollback signals do you use during ramp?
summary: VertexWave reviewed Redwood’s workload-aware batching defaults and specifically evaluated the cost-efficient tier for cost reduction on non-interactive workloads. Discussion centered on (1) how Redwood defines the fast/standard/cost-efficient latency SLO tiers and what knobs are affected (max batch size, max queue delay, prefill/decode scheduling weights, KV cache pressure), (2) streaming token cadence risks and mitigations, and (3) Redwood’s benchmark methodology (workload corpus, concurrency sweeps, and regression thresholds) plus rollout/rollback criteria. VertexWave asked to run a small pilot: cost-efficient on background summarization/non-streaming routes while keeping fast/standard for interactive streaming chat.

transcript_text:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: VertexWave x Redwood — Tiered batching + cost-efficient tier technical deep dive
Date: 2025-02-14
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Aditya Rao, Sofia Ivanova, Sean Gallagher, Jonas Weber
VertexWave: Evan Liu, Priya Shah, Marta González, Tom Becker

---

[00:00] Aditya Rao: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is Aditya from Redwood. I know this one is meant to be pretty technical — batching tiers, the new defaults, and specifically the “cost-efficient” tier you asked about.

[00:12] Evan Liu: Yep. Thanks. We’re trying to take cost out of a couple routes. Interactive chat is one thing, but we have a bunch of background summarization and re-ranking style jobs. We saw the mention of cost-efficient tier in the beta notes and wanted to understand what it actually does.

[00:30] Aditya Rao: Makes sense. Quick intros — Sofia leads runtime scheduling for us. Sean is SRE SLO owner. Jonas does evals/quality gating for changes like this.

[00:41] Sofia Ivanova: Hey everyone.

[00:42] Sean Gallagher: Hi.

[00:44] Jonas Weber: Hello.

[00:46] Priya Shah: Hi, Priya here, ML engineer. I’ll probably ask annoying questions about what you measure.

[00:52] Marta González: Marta, SRE. I’m mostly here for the SLO and “how do we not page ourselves” part.

[00:58] Tom Becker: Tom, engineering manager. I’m here to make sure we can roll this without, you know, surprises.

---

[01:10] Aditya Rao: Awesome. Let’s anchor on what the tiers are. We’re standardizing on three batching profiles — fast, standard, cost-efficient. The idea is: customers pick a tier as a default posture, and we map that to scheduler knobs. You can still override explicit knobs if you want, but the tier is meant to be safe-by-default.

[01:33] Evan Liu: When you say “scheduler knobs,” what does that include? Is it just max batch size?

[01:38] Sofia Ivanova: It’s a bundle. The main ones: (1) maximum batch size and token budget, (2) maximum queue delay — like how long we’ll wait to form a batch before we run, (3) prefill vs decode scheduling weights — that affects time-to-first-token and token cadence, (4) admission control thresholds and some KV cache pressure limits so we don’t OOM under high concurrency.

[02:02] Priya Shah: So cost-efficient is basically “wait longer to build bigger batches,” right?

[02:06] Sofia Ivanova: Broadly yes, but we also change how aggressively we prioritize decode to avoid the “streaming feels chunky” problem. Cost-efficient makes sense for non-streaming routes, or where you care about throughput dollars, not minimum latency.

[02:20] Sean Gallagher: And from SRE side, each tier has defined SLO targets and acceptable regressions. We don’t just turn knobs and hope.

---

[02:33] Marta González: Can you be explicit about the SLO definitions? Like p95, p99, what window, and what is measured exactly.

[02:40] Sean Gallagher: Yep. For our purposes, the primary is end-to-end request latency — from request accepted to final token emitted (or response completed). We also track TTFT — time to first token — for streaming. Windows: we look at rolling 5-minute and 30-minute, with burn-rate alerts in the 30-minute for paging. p95 and p99 are both tracked; the tier contract is mostly p95, but p99 is used as a rollback signal.

[03:08] Marta González: That’s aligned with us. We page on p99 spikes, p95 is more like “is the system healthy.”

[03:12] Sean Gallagher: Exactly.

[03:14] Evan Liu: For cost-efficient tier, what p95 are you targeting? Like, what are the numbers.

[03:19] Sean Gallagher: It depends on model family and region/GPU SKU. But conceptually:
- Fast tier: optimized for interactive. Low queue delay, stricter scheduling on decode.
- Standard: balanced — what most customers run.
- Cost-efficient: allows more queue delay and larger effective batches; you should expect higher p95, but lower $/token.

[03:42] Evan Liu: That’s a little vague. Are we talking +10% p95 or 2x?

[03:47] Sofia Ivanova: For non-streaming jobs, we’ve seen cost-efficient give ~15–35% cost reduction with p95 latency increases typically in the 10–30% range at moderate concurrency. At very low traffic, cost-efficient can actually look worse because you’re waiting to batch but there’s nobody to batch with.

[04:08] Priya Shah: That’s important. We have diurnal patterns — overnight is low.

[04:12] Sofia Ivanova: Right, so the workload-aware part matters. We use signals like prompt length buckets and observed concurrency, plus whether you’re streaming. If concurrency is low, we cap queue delay and we don’t chase a batch size that never forms.

[04:28] Evan Liu: Do you actually detect concurrency in real time? Or is it a static setting.

[04:32] Sofia Ivanova: We detect it at the runtime level (per replica / per model pool) using the in-flight queue and service time estimates. It’s not a new research scheduler — it’s more like “don’t apply cost-efficient queue delays blindly if you’re underutilized.”

---

[05:00] Aditya Rao: Maybe it’s helpful if we split your workloads. Evan, you mentioned interactive chat and background summarization. Are those separate routes?

[05:08] Evan Liu: Yep. /chat is streaming, /summarize is non-streaming, /extract is non-streaming. We also have some embeddings but that’s separate.

[05:17] Aditya Rao: Great. The common pattern is: keep /chat on fast or standard, and put /summarize and /extract on cost-efficient.

[05:26] Priya Shah: Can we do per-route tier selection? Like in config.

[05:30] Aditya Rao: Yes. You can set it per deployment and also per route/policy. Console will show a dropdown per route once enabled. For API, you can specify the tier in the config for that endpoint.

[05:44] Evan Liu: And if we already have explicit batching settings, what happens.

[05:47] Sofia Ivanova: Explicit overrides win. Tier sets defaults; explicit settings override. We also expose an “effective config” in debug so you can see what’s actually being applied, because precedence confusion is common.

[06:01] Marta González: Thank you. That’s exactly the thing that creates incidents.

---

[06:10] Priya Shah: Let’s talk streaming cadence. We had a bad experience with vLLM batching where token streaming came in bursts and the UI looked frozen, even though throughput was high.

[06:22] Sofia Ivanova: Yep. That’s the primary risk. If decode gets deprioritized because you’re always pre-filling a bigger batch, you can hurt token cadence. In fast tier we heavily prioritize decode; in standard we balance; in cost-efficient we still protect decode for streaming but we assume streaming is not the target.

[06:42] Evan Liu: But could someone accidentally set cost-efficient on a streaming route and not notice?

[06:47] Aditya Rao: We try to guardrail that. In docs we’re going to say “don’t use cost-efficient for streaming unless you’ve validated cadence.” And we can put warnings in Console.

[06:59] Sean Gallagher: Also, streaming routes have extra rollback signals: TTFT and “tokens per second to client” distribution. If those regress beyond threshold in canary, we roll back.

[07:12] Marta González: “Tokens per second to client” — you measure that?

[07:15] Sean Gallagher: We measure inter-token intervals and aggregate. Not perfect, but it catches the chunky streaming pattern.

[07:23] Priya Shah: Is that per request or across the fleet.

[07:26] Sean Gallagher: Both; per request histograms and fleet-level percentiles.

---

[07:40] Evan Liu: Can you define queue delay precisely? Like what is it. Is it time in a queue before being scheduled.

[07:47] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly. For a request, queue delay is time between admission and when the request is included in a batch execution. We break it into: waiting-to-form-batch and scheduling wait if the GPU is busy.

[08:04] Priya Shah: And cost-efficient raises the max queue delay.

[08:06] Sofia Ivanova: Yes, but bounded. There’s a tier-specific max_queue_delay_ms and then we also cap by request deadline / timeout budget.

[08:17] Marta González: That last part matters — we have 30s timeouts at the gateway.

[08:21] Sofia Ivanova: Yep. If your timeout is 30s, we’re not going to wait, say, 2s to batch if you’re already in a tail latency situation. We also have overload protection: if queue is growing, we can shed or backpressure rather than keep adding queue delay and causing p99 to blow up.

[08:42] Evan Liu: Okay. In practice, what max queue delay numbers are we talking about.

[08:47] Sofia Ivanova: Rough guidance (not a promise): fast is on the order of single-digit ms, standard is tens of ms, cost-efficient can be higher — think tens to low hundreds ms — for non-streaming, depending on model and GPU.

[09:06] Evan Liu: Got it.

---

[09:10] Aditya Rao: Let’s shift to benchmark methodology because that was in your email.

[09:14] Priya Shah: Yes. We’ve been burned by “benchmarks” that don’t match our prompts. What is your corpus.

[09:22] Jonas Weber: The corpus is a mix: multi-turn chat traces, short and medium prompts, and some long-context prompts. We bucket by prompt length and expected completion length. For each model family we run concurrency sweeps — like 1, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc — and we record p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput tokens/sec, and cost proxies like GPU time per token.

[09:48] Priya Shah: Do you include tool calls / function calling.

[09:51] Jonas Weber: We include some structured output patterns. Tool calling can change token distributions (short completions, more starts/stops). We treat it as a workload type. For the initial tier defaults, the major focus is chat + summarization + extraction.

[10:11] Evan Liu: And how do you avoid quality regressions? Batching shouldn’t change output, but sampling can be nondeterministic.

[10:19] Jonas Weber: Correct. Batching changes timing and can change floating point order in some kernels, which can move logits slightly. So our quality gate uses a prompt set with fixed seeds and compares distributions. We have thresholds for exact match where possible and semantic similarity/score deltas where not. We also do A/B sampling in canary — if quality metrics move outside bounds, it’s a rollback trigger.

[10:46] Priya Shah: That’s good. We also use a fixed set with human-reviewed outcomes.

---

[10:55] Marta González: From ops side, what dashboards would we watch in a pilot.

[11:01] Sean Gallagher: For tiered batching, the core ones:
1) Latency p50/p95/p99 per route and per tier label.
2) Queue delay histogram, also per route.
3) Batch size distribution and batch formation rate.
4) GPU utilization and memory pressure / KV cache utilization.
5) Timeout and cancellation rates.
6) For streaming: TTFT and inter-token interval.

[11:28] Marta González: And alert thresholds are tier-specific?

[11:31] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. We don’t want cost-efficient to page you the same way fast does, but we do want to page on increased error rates, and on unexpected tail blow-ups.

[11:42] Evan Liu: We’d probably run it on a subset first anyway.

[11:45] Aditya Rao: That’s the right approach.

---

[12:00] Evan Liu: Can you talk about rollout controls. Is it a feature flag, or config.

[12:06] Aditya Rao: Both. Tier selection is config. But the new workload-aware defaults are behind a flag during beta. We can enable it for specific models/regions and even do percentage-based ramp.

[12:20] Tom Becker: Percentage ramp by traffic or by accounts.

[12:23] Aditya Rao: Typically by account and model/region. If you’re on Hosted API, we can do it at the control plane. If Dedicated/Private, you can do it via config + our rollout tooling.

[12:38] Tom Becker: And rollback is automatic or manual.

[12:41] Sean Gallagher: We have automatic rollback hooks if key metrics cross thresholds in canary, and manual kill-switch for on-call.

---

[13:00] Priya Shah: Let’s get more concrete. For our summarize route: typical prompt is 1–2k tokens, completion like 200–500 tokens. Concurrency maybe 10–20 during the day, can spike to 50.

[13:16] Sofia Ivanova: That’s a good fit for cost-efficient. Longer prefill cost means batching helps a lot. But the risk is KV cache memory at high concurrency. We’ve added tier-specific KV cache pressure limits — if we get close to OOM we’ll clamp batch formation and prefer smaller batches.

[13:38] Evan Liu: Wait, how does that interplay with max batch size.

[13:41] Sofia Ivanova: Think of max batch as an upper bound. The effective batch size is also limited by token budget and memory pressure heuristics. In cost-efficient we allow higher targets, but we won’t exceed safe memory thresholds.

[13:56] Priya Shah: Do you expose those thresholds.

[13:58] Sofia Ivanova: Some of them, yes — especially ones customers might override. Some internal safety rails are fixed per model/GPU, but we can share the effective config output so you can see what was chosen.

---

[14:20] Evan Liu: How do we validate the cost savings? We care about $ per 1M tokens.

[14:25] Aditya Rao: We report token-level cost and latency breakdowns in Console. For Hosted, you’ll see billed tokens obviously, but the savings are from reduced GPU time. We show an estimate: GPU-ms per token and effective throughput.

[14:43] Evan Liu: So you’ll give us like “you would have spent X on standard and Y on cost-efficient.”

[14:47] Aditya Rao: Exactly — comparative view based on measured utilization and request mix.

[14:55] Marta González: That’s helpful for us to justify switching.

---

[15:10] Priya Shah: Back to streaming. Our /chat route is streaming; we care about TTFT under 800ms p95 and then steady token cadence.

[15:21] Sean Gallagher: Then I’d recommend fast for /chat. Standard can work if you’re cost-sensitive but you’ll need to validate cadence.

[15:30] Sofia Ivanova: Also note: if you have multi-turn chat with long context, prefill dominates and you can hurt TTFT if you batch too much. Fast tier uses low queue delay and decode-prioritization.

[15:44] Evan Liu: Is fast tier more expensive.

[15:46] Aditya Rao: Typically yes — you’re sacrificing some batching efficiency for latency.

---

[16:05] Tom Becker: What’s the “workload-aware” part exactly. Are you doing like ML to pick parameters.

[16:11] Sofia Ivanova: No ML. It’s heuristics + guardrails. We look at request characteristics (prompt length bucket, streaming flag), concurrency, and model family. Then we pick one of a small set of parameter mappings per tier.

[16:30] Tom Becker: Okay. That’s good — simpler.

---

[16:40] Evan Liu: We’ve also considered AWS Bedrock for some routes. They have their own throttling and performance characteristics. How do you compare.

[16:49] Aditya Rao: Bedrock is great if you want managed. Our differentiation is you get more control over inference economics and consistent behavior across hosted, dedicated, private. Also, you can pick tier defaults and see effective config; Bedrock is more opaque.

[17:06] Evan Liu: Right now, we’re on a mix of OpenAI for some stuff and self-host vLLM for others.

[17:13] Aditya Rao: That’s pretty common.

---

[17:20] Marta González: For the pilot, we’d want a clear rollback trigger list. Can you share what you use.

[17:27] Sean Gallagher: For cost-efficient tier on non-streaming routes:
- p95 latency regression beyond agreed threshold (we typically start with 15–20% allowed, but you can pick).
- p99 spikes sustained.
- Error rate increases (5xx, timeouts, cancellations) beyond baseline + delta.
- Queue delay p99 crossing a hard cap for sustained window.
- GPU memory OOM events (should be zero).
For streaming routes, add TTFT and cadence metrics.

[17:58] Marta González: Great.

---

[18:05] Priya Shah: One more question: does batching impact determinism. We have tests that assume stable outputs.

[18:12] Jonas Weber: It can, slightly. If you need strict determinism, you should run with deterministic settings and accept some performance hit. For typical sampling, we treat small deltas as acceptable but we gate on semantic/score regressions.

[18:30] Priya Shah: Okay.

---

[18:35] Evan Liu: If we opt into cost-efficient on summarize, what do we need to change.

[18:40] Aditya Rao: Minimal. You’d set batching_tier=cost_efficient for that route. If you have existing explicit batching config, we’ll need to confirm what you want — keep overrides or let tier set defaults.

[18:55] Evan Liu: We currently set max_batch to 8, and queue delay I think 10ms.

[19:00] Sofia Ivanova: That’s fairly conservative. Cost-efficient would likely raise those, but again, it depends.

[19:07] Evan Liu: We did that because we were afraid of tail latency.

[19:10] Sean Gallagher: That’s reasonable. Cost-efficient should come with overload protection and clearer SLO expectations, so you don’t have to guess.

---

[19:25] Priya Shah: Can you share a sample benchmark report. Like a table.

[19:30] Aditya Rao: Yep. We can share a redacted sample: fast vs standard vs cost-efficient for a representative model, showing p95, throughput, and $/token estimate.

[19:41] Evan Liu: That would be useful internally.

---

[20:00] (crosstalk)
[20:01] Marta González: Sorry, one more.
[20:02] Sofia Ivanova: Go ahead.

[20:04] Marta González: How do you prevent queue delay metrics from being noisy. We had alerts that fired on histograms being weird.

[20:12] Sean Gallagher: Yeah, queue delay is noisy. We don’t alert on raw p95 of queue delay alone. We alert when it correlates with request latency or timeouts, and we apply burn-rate style alerts. Also we label by tier and route to avoid mixing distributions.

[20:32] Marta González: Perfect.

---

[21:00] Aditya Rao: Let’s align on a proposed plan. For VertexWave:
- Keep /chat on fast.
- Put /summarize and /extract on cost-efficient.
- Run 10% traffic ramp during daytime peak first.
- Watch dashboards for p95/p99, queue delay, timeouts.
- Compare cost metrics over 24–48 hours.

[21:23] Evan Liu: That seems right. We’d need your guidance on what “10%” means in config.

[21:28] Aditya Rao: We’ll send instructions. For Hosted, we can apply it per account on our side; you can also do it per route. If you want to do it yourself, we can expose a policy rule.

[21:42] Tom Becker: And we can opt out quickly if things go wrong.

[21:45] Aditya Rao: Yes.

---

[22:05] Priya Shah: For workload-aware signals, you mentioned prompt length buckets. Do you expose the buckets.

[22:12] Sofia Ivanova: We expose the bucket label in metrics. E.g., prompt_len_bucket. It’s coarse — like 0–256, 256–1k, 1k–4k, etc.

[22:25] Priya Shah: Great. We can correlate with our own.

---

[23:00] Evan Liu: How model-specific are the defaults. If we switch from one model family to another, does tier mapping change.

[23:08] Sofia Ivanova: Yes, it can. Prefill cost differs across architectures and context length. We store per-model-family defaults and sometimes per GPU SKU. The tier name is stable, but the numeric values can differ.

[23:27] Evan Liu: That’s okay as long as it’s transparent.

[23:31] Aditya Rao: That’s why we’re investing in effective config explainers.

---

[24:00] Marta González: Do you provide audit logs when tier changes.

[24:05] Aditya Rao: Yes — for enterprise accounts, tier changes are in audit logs (who/when/what). That’s part of the change management story.

[24:15] Marta González: Nice.

---

[25:00] (discussion continues; minor audio drop)

[25:06] Evan Liu: Sorry, you cut out for a second. Did you say you can show “effective config” in headers?

[25:12] Aditya Rao: Potentially. Today, we can expose it via an endpoint and in Console; we’ve also experimented with returning a debug header for staging. We’ll confirm what’s available for your account.

[25:30] Evan Liu: That would help us debug.

---

[26:10] Priya Shah: Any known limitations with cost-efficient tier.

[26:14] Sofia Ivanova: Two main ones:
1) Low traffic: you won’t form batches, so you just add delay. Workload-aware heuristics mitigate but don’t magically create traffic.
2) Streaming: not recommended without careful validation.
Also, very long-context workloads can hit memory pressure faster; we added guardrails but we still advise monitoring.

[26:43] Priya Shah: Makes sense.

---

[27:10] Aditya Rao: I want to respect time. Anything else you want to cover.

[27:15] Evan Liu: I think we have enough to proceed. We’ll need the follow-up email with opt-in and the benchmark methodology. Also we’ll share our histograms.

[27:26] Marta González: Plus a list of metrics and what “good” looks like. Even if it’s just “watch these charts.”

[27:33] Sean Gallagher: Yep, we’ll send a pilot monitoring checklist.

[27:40] Priya Shah: And maybe a quick note on determinism and expected output drift.

[27:45] Jonas Weber: I’ll send guidance.

---

[28:00] Aditya Rao: Great. Next steps: I’ll send opt-in instructions and a suggested tier-by-route plan. Sofia will share the streaming cadence / metrics validation notes. Sean will share dashboards to watch and rollback triggers. You’ll share your sanitized workload profile.

[28:18] Evan Liu: Sounds good.

[28:20] Aditya Rao: Thanks everyone.

[28:22] (Call continues with informal Q&A / scheduling for remainder of recording; transcription below is partial and includes some minor cross-talk.)

[29:05] Tom Becker: Are you able to join our internal review next week, like 30 minutes.

[29:10] Aditya Rao: Yes, probably. Send times.

[29:12] Evan Liu: Tuesday or Wednesday.

[29:15] Aditya Rao: Cool.

[30:02] Priya Shah: One last thing — can we run a quick A/B with the same prompts.

[30:06] Jonas Weber: Yes, that’s our recommendation. Use fixed prompt set and compare latency + output deltas.

[31:20] Marta González: If we see timeouts, what do you want from us.

[31:23] Sean Gallagher: Request IDs, route, tier label, and approximate timestamp. Also whether you saw increased queue delay vs compute time.

[33:40] Evan Liu: Ok.

[35:05] Sofia Ivanova: And if you can, share prompt length and max tokens settings.

[36:12] Evan Liu: Yep.

[40:30] (scheduling / wrap-up)

[57:40] Aditya Rao: Alright, we’ll follow up. Thanks again.

---

Auto-notes (generated)
- Customer evaluating cost-efficient tier for non-streaming routes; keep fast tier for streaming chat.
- Key risks discussed: queue delay and streaming cadence.
- Redwood to provide benchmark methodology + monitoring checklist + opt-in steps.
